title: A money type with standard traits
description:
Write a `Money` type (whole cents in an `i64`) that behaves like a built-in number:

```rust
#[derive(...)]                               // Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Default
struct Money(i64);

impl Display for Money                       // "12.34", "-0.05", "1000.00"
impl FromStr for Money                       // "12.34", "-5", "0.5", "+3.10"; at most 2 decimals; Err(String) otherwise
impl Add, Sub for Money; impl Mul<i64> for Money; impl Neg for Money
impl std::iter::Sum for Money               // so that an iterator of Money can be .sum()-ed
impl From<i64> for Money                     // whole euros: Money::from(5) is 5.00
```
hints: Derive what can be derived (`Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Default`); write `Display`, `FromStr`, the operators, `Sum` and `From` by hand.

`Sum` has one method, which receives any iterator of `Money`: `impl Sum for Money { fn sum<I: Iterator<Item = Money>>(iter: I) -> Money { ... } }`. Inside, a `for m in iter` loop can add them up with your `Add`.
For parsing, split off a sign, then split at the `.`; check that both parts are digits and that there are at most two decimals; pad the decimals to two digits (`"5"` means 50 cents).
